summary: Defines the Clearance attribute, which states what clearance a certificate subject holds, and the Authority Clearance Constraints extension, which limits the effective clearance a subject can have along a certification path. These can appear in X.509 public key and attribute certificates. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Like a badge showing which secret rooms you may enter, plus a rule that lets the badge-issuer limit it. This puts those badge details inside digital certificates.

questions: what is the x.509 clearance attribute
what is the x509 clearance attribute
how is effective clearance computed in a certification path
subtitle: How X.509 certificates carry security clearances and how authorities can cap the clearances they vouch for.

tldr.problem: Organizations with a security policy want certificates to state the clearance a subject holds, and want a CA or AA to limit which clearances relying parties accept from it.
tldr.mechanism: A Clearance attribute states the policy, classification levels and extra categories. An Authority Clearance Constraints extension in trust anchors, CAs and AAs is intersected along the certification path to give the effective clearance.
tldr.outcome: A relying party gets an effective clearance that can never exceed what the subject's certificate claims or what any authority on the path permits.

facts.label: Clearance attributes per certificate
facts.value: Zero or one, with a single value

today: RFC 5913 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Clearances in Certificates
sections.content:
Organizations with a security policy can issue certificates that state the clearance held by the subject. The Clearance attribute names the security policy, the clearance levels and additional authorization information. Its ASN.1 syntax comes from RFC 5912. It can sit in the subject directory attributes extension of a public key certificate (PKC) or in an attribute certificate (AC).

The RFC says PKCs suit relatively static clearances that can be verified at issuance, or cases where credentials must be revoked when clearance changes. ACs suit more dynamic clearances whose change should not force revocation of PKCs. It names the Defense Messaging Service as an example of clearances in PKCs in an operational PKI.

This document augments the certification path validation rules of RFC 5280 for PKCs and RFC 5755 for ACs.
sections.eli5: A certificate is like an ID card. This lets the card also say how secret a thing its owner is allowed to see.

sections.title: The Clearance Attribute
sections.content:
A certificate MUST include zero or one Clearance attribute, and if present it MUST hold a single value. The attribute is identified by id-at-clearance. It is a SEQUENCE of three fields, with meanings taken from Section 4.4.6 of RFC 5755:

  • policyId: the security policy the clearance relates to. It sets the meaning of the other two fields.
  • classList: a bit string of classifications. Six basic bits are defined: unmarked (0), unclassified (1), restricted (2), confidential (3), secret (4) and topSecret (5). A policy may define more. The default is unclassified.
  • securityCategories: optional extra authorization information.

If a trust anchor's public key is used directly, the clearance associated with that trust anchor, if any, should be used as the effective clearance.
sections.eli5: The badge says which rulebook applies, how high your secrecy level is, and any extra special-access stamps you hold.

sections.title: Authority Clearance Constraints
sections.content:
This extension tells a relying party which clearances are acceptable for the subject of an AC or for the last certificate in a PKC path. It is only meaningful in a trust anchor (TA), a CA PKC or an AA PKC, each of which MUST include zero or one instance. It MAY be critical or non-critical.

Its value is a sequence of one or more Clearance entries, which the authority asserts. The sequence MUST NOT hold two entries with the same policyId; if it does, the certification path is rejected. If the extension is absent, that TA, CA or AA does not constrain clearance.

For example, a CA for a company policy with three classification values could carry the extension so that it is constrained to just one of them. Cross-certified domains can use it too.
sections.eli5: A badge-issuer can add a rule saying, I only vouch for the lowest rooms. Nobody under that issuer can get more than the rule allows.

sections.title: Computing the Effective Clearance
sections.content:
The effective clearance of the subject is the intersection of four things: the Clearance attribute in the subject's certificate, the constraints in the trust anchor, user input, and the constraints in all intermediate PKCs. For an AC, the constraints come from the TA and every PKC up to and including the AA PKC. Any algorithm giving the same outcome is compliant.

Processing keeps one state variable, permitted-clearances. It starts as the user input, or the special value all-clearances if none is given. Each extension met along the path, starting with the trust anchor, narrows it. In the final step the subject's Clearance is intersected with it.

The result is the effective clearance, which can be an empty list, plus success or failure with a reason code. Failures include multiple instances of an attribute, multiple values, and multiple instances of the same clearance.
sections.eli5: Imagine passing your badge through several gates. Each gate crosses out anything it does not allow, and what is left at the end is what you may really do.

sections.title: Intersection Rules
sections.content:
When a PKC carries the extension and permitted-clearances is not all-clearances, each clearance already permitted is checked. If its policyId is missing from the new extension, it is deleted. Otherwise each classList bit stays one only if it is one in both, and if no bits remain the clearance is deleted. If permitted-clearances is still all-clearances, it simply takes the extension's value.

The securityCategories intersection keeps identical elements, and for elements of the same type OID with known semantics it does a type-specific intersection. The algorithm is idempotent, associative and commutative. The RFC also gives an example category: a bit string identified by an OID, where the intersection sets the bits set in both values. It is only an example until an OID is registered and the bits are defined.
sections.eli5: Only the things that appear on every list survive. If something is missing from one list, it drops out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Issuers must remember that a missing Authority Clearance Constraints extension in a TA, CA or AA certificate means the authority is not constrained in terms of clearance. A missing Clearance attribute means the subject has no clearance assigned, and a trust anchor with no clearance has none assigned either.

If local policy treats a subject's clearance, or the clearances an authority supports, as sensitive, the attribute and extension should only be included if the certificates can be privacy protected. Distribution of trust anchors and their constraints or clearances must be privacy protected too.
sections.eli5: No rule does not mean no rights: it means no limit from that issuer. If the badge details are secret, the badges must be kept private too.
